sketches.title: The Fine Print
sketches.premise: You make a New Year's resolution. The host reads the loophole that ruins it, then you add the next loophole. Keep the promise technically alive while making it increasingly useless.
sketches.criterion: A move follows if it is one plain new condition caused by the current wording and weakens the resolution without actually canceling it; a skipped link jumps to a later loophole, an ending makes the promise fully honored or abandoned, and an undo removes or reverses a condition already added.
sketches.move_shape: Start with a resolution, then add one dry fine-print clause beginning with “Except when…” or “As long as…”. Example: “I will stop eating junk food.” — “Except food is not junk if it came in a paper bag.”
sketches.first_card: I will get fit this year.

sketches.title: The Apology Tour
sketches.premise: Your resolution has already gone slightly wrong, and the host gives a flat press statement about it. On each turn, add one new fact that makes the public explanation harder to believe while keeping the speaker talking.
sketches.criterion: A move follows if it is one new, observable fact that directly makes the latest statement look worse and forces the next explanation; a skipped link invents a distant scandal, an ending gives a final confession or clears the speaker, and an undo retracts a fact already stated.
sketches.move_shape: Give one host-style statement beginning with “The official position is…” and add one fact, not a feeling or verdict. Example: “The official position is that I am saving money.” — “The bank statement contains a charge for a life-size inflatable hot tub.”
sketches.first_card: The official position is that I am finally taking work seriously.

sketches.title: People v. Good Intentions
sketches.premise: A resolution is on trial for collapsing in public. The host presents one piece of evidence, and the other player adds the next piece, until the promise is either exposed as nonsense or somehow survives. The defendant is the resolution, not you; relax, you are only the witness being mocked.
sketches.criterion: A move follows if it is one concrete piece of evidence caused by the previous exhibit and makes the resolution harder to defend; a skipped link introduces a new charge without evidence, an ending gives the verdict, and an undo contradicts or removes admitted evidence.
sketches.move_shape: State one exhibit in the form “Exhibit [number]: …”, with a visible object, message, or action. Example: “Exhibit A: My running shoes are still in their box.” — “Exhibit B: The box is being used to store crisps.”
sketches.first_card: Exhibit A: The calendar says I planned to wake up early.

sketches.title: Please Hold for Change
sketches.premise: You contact an imaginary help desk because your New Year's resolution is not working. The host gives one boring support reply, and you add the next problem that the reply creates. Escalate through menus, tickets, and useless fixes without solving the original promise.
sketches.criterion: A move follows if it is one new support problem plainly caused by the latest reply and keeps the resolution active; a skipped link jumps to a dramatic failure, an ending solves, closes, or cancels the ticket, and an undo restores a menu or fix that was already rejected.
sketches.move_shape: Write one support exchange: “Support: … / Customer: …”, with the customer’s line caused by support’s last line. Example: “Support: Please reset your password. / Customer: The reset email went to the account I am trying to recover.”
sketches.first_card: Support: Welcome to Resolution Support. What seems to be the problem?

sketches.title: The Responsible Choice
sketches.premise: You are trying to follow a resolution at home, while the host calmly adds household rules that make it harder. Each turn adds one rule or object interaction that bends the promise toward a ridiculous but still legal result.
sketches.criterion: A move follows if it is one household event directly triggered by the latest rule or object and makes the resolution less useful without breaking it outright; a skipped link brings in an unrelated room or result, an ending makes the resolution succeed or fail completely, and an undo removes a rule or returns an object to its earlier state.
sketches.move_shape: Add one house rule beginning with “For safety…” and show its immediate effect on one named object. Example: “For safety, the biscuits must be kept out of reach.” — “The biscuits go on top of the fridge, beside the emergency biscuits.”
sketches.first_card: For safety, my new exercise plan starts with one gentle stretch.

sketches.title: New Year, New Logo
sketches.premise: Your resolution is being relaunched as a product after its first version starts failing. The host gives dry brand commentary, and each turn adds one visible update that makes the product sound better while making the promise less real. No one is allowed to admit the product is dead; marketing would hate that.
sketches.criterion: A move follows if it is one concrete rebrand caused by the current product problem and preserves a recognizable piece of the original resolution; a skipped link adds a final redesign without its failed version, an ending retires or successfully launches the product, and an undo restores an older brand version.
sketches.move_shape: Give one update in the form “New feature: …”, naming a change that responds to the previous failure. Example: “New feature: the budgeting app now calls every purchase a wellness investment.”
sketches.first_card: New feature: the fitness plan begins with a calendar and a confident color scheme.
